items.title: Evan Christopher interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 1, 2009
items.q: most of the veterans are gone, and there’s only a handful out there that are still getting thousands of dollars for their appearances: Hank Jones and Ornette Coleman.

ctx.x: Yeah. I’m going to ask you one more question that we can dub in. I’m expecting our tape to run out. I forget the circumstances, it might have been in one of the classes yesterday, you were talking about Lincoln Center and sort of this striving to make jazz, to bring it up to the level of how people think about classical music. And I’m wondering if that’s sort of a fool’s errand, because the musics are not the same — I can’t even finish my question.

I think it’s a double edged sword to try to — look we’re in the period where there’s a level of alienation from the arts in general that’s high enough that I don’t think we need to make it worse by re-framing jazz or by continuing this track of framing it as a higher art. I mean I think all of it needs to be brought down through education, that’s how I would do it, to a level where the function of the music is not only more evident but viewed as essential. I think it’s not only jazz that needs to be returned to…

obligatory cultural experiences. But I think classical music needs to kind of have the same battle. I think especially when the economy is like this. You can’t continue to kind of act like the audience’s concerns aren’t important in a way, as if what you’re doing is so important that oh, they’ll come when they figure it out. You know I think we need to equally present ourselves as artists. Not just jazz, but I think we need to put ourselves on doorsteps for people and say here we are. Like we can help you. This…
